text: Every circuit you've built so far has been a building block. This chapter shows you where those blocks go when you assemble them into named, well-known quantum algorithms — and the first thing you need to know is that the library providing them is not where older tutorials say it is.

If you've read older Qiskit tutorials, you may have seen code importing from qiskit dot algorithms. That import no longer works. As of Qiskit 1.0, that module was removed from the core qiskit package entirely — the implementations moved into a separate, still-actively-maintained package called qiskit-algorithms, which you install and import on its own.

This chapter covers four things. Amplitude amplification and search — Grover and AmplificationProblem, which generalize Grover's algorithm to boost the probability of measuring a marked outcome. Variational algorithms — VQE and QAOA, pairing a parameterized circuit with a classical optimizer. And amplitude estimation, building on the same amplification mechanics as Grover. Notably absent from that list: the Quantum Fourier Transform.

It's tempting to assume every named algorithm lives in qiskit-algorithms, but the QFT is a circuit, not a search or optimization routine — so it ships as part of core qiskit's circuit library. QFT of num_qubits equals 3 returns a ready-to-use circuit, because the QFT is really a reusable building block other algorithms, like Shor's algorithm and phase estimation, call as a subroutine.

Every algorithm in this library is built from exactly the same pieces you already know: circuits you build with QuantumCircuit, a primitive for execution — Sampler for outcome probabilities, Estimator for expectation values — and sometimes a classical optimizer, only for variational algorithms that iterate between quantum evaluation and classical parameter updates. Grover's algorithm, stripped down, is a circuit with an oracle and a diffuser run through a Sampler. Nothing here requires new quantum mechanics beyond what you already have.
Next lesson builds the smallest possible Grover circuit by hand, gate by gate, so you can see exactly how the quadratic speedup happens before reaching for the library version.
